---
title: "The render list: choosing which files render"
---

## Overview

When you run `q2 render` on a project, Quarto builds a **render
list**: the set of source files that become pages of your site. You
control it with the `project.render` key in `_quarto.yml`:

```yaml
project:
  type: website
  render:
    - "**/*.qmd"
    - "!drafts/**"
```

Each entry is a glob, matched against paths relative to the project
root. Entries starting with `!` are exclusions; an exclusion applies
to the whole list, wherever it appears. A bare directory name means
everything renderable beneath it.

## The default

Omitting `project.render` is exactly equivalent to writing:

```yaml
project:
  render:
    - "**/*.qmd"
```

That is: every `.qmd` file in the project, wherever it lives. A render
list containing only exclusions subtracts from that same default —
`render: ["!drafts/**"]` means "all `.qmd` files except those under
`drafts/`".

Quarto renders `.qmd` by default and nothing else. Every other input
type must be listed:

| Input | Rendered by default? |
|-------|----------------------|
| `.qmd` | yes |
| `.md` | only when a pattern matches it |
| `.ipynb` | only when a pattern matches it |
| `.py` / `.R` scripts | only when a pattern matches it |
| file types added by an extension | only when a pattern matches it |

A positive pattern replaces the default; it does not add to it. Keep
`"**/*.qmd"` in any list you write, or your `.qmd` files stop
rendering:

```yaml
project:
  render:
    - "**/*.qmd"      # keep this
    - "**/*.ipynb"
```

## Rendering `.md` files

Plain Markdown files can be full members of a Quarto project — they
support the complete Quarto markdown dialect (shortcodes, divs,
cross-references, navigation, themes) and render exactly like `.qmd`
files, with one difference: **`.md` files never execute code**.

`.md` files are opt-in: they render only when a `project.render`
pattern you wrote matches them. Add them alongside your `.qmd` globs:

```yaml
project:
  render:
    - "**/*.qmd"
    - "**/*.md"
    - "!news/NEWS.md"
```

Any pattern you write can opt them in — `chapters/*`, a literal
`notes.md`, or an extension glob all work. What never opts them in is
the default: a project without a `render:` key renders `.qmd` only.

Because `.md` files never execute code, an `engine:` specification in
a `.md` file's front matter has no effect. Quarto warns about it
([`Q-2-40`](/errors/markdown/Q-2-40.qmd)) and renders the document
without execution; rename the file to `.qmd` if you need executable
code.

### Why other file types are opt-in

Quarto 1 built its render list by walking the whole project and asking
each execution engine whether it claimed each file. The Markdown engine
claimed `.md` unconditionally. The Jupyter engine claimed `.ipynb`, and
opened every `.py` to see whether it held `# %%` cells. The knitr engine
opened every `.R` looking for a `#'` header.

Quarto 2 does not inspect files to decide what to render. The render
list comes from patterns alone.

Two consequences. A stray `NEWS.md`, a `conftest.py`, or a scratch
notebook stays out of the render list until you ask for it. And
installing an extension never changes which files your project
renders — only what Quarto can do with them once listed.

### Listed scripts with a declared processor

Once a script *is* listed, Quarto still has to turn it into a
document. For the two script formats Quarto understands natively, that
conversion happens in-process — no execution engine is launched to
decide what the file is:

- **Percent scripts** — cells delimited by comment lines such as
  `# %%` (the format Jupytext and VS Code popularized), in Python,
  Julia, R, and other `#`-comment languages.
- **Spin scripts** — an R script whose `#'` lines are prose and whose
  remaining code becomes executable chunks, in the style of knitr's
  `spin()`.

The built-in Jupyter and knitr engines declare these conversions
statically, so a listed `.py`, `.jl`, or `.R` script is recognized and
converted without launching anything — and an error in the rendered
page points back at the original script's file, line, and column.

An engine extension declares the same thing on a `claims-files` entry
in its `_extension.yml`, with the `processor:` key:

```yaml
contributes:
  engines:
    - name: myengine
      claims-files:
        - extension: .jl
          processor: { name: percent, language: julia }
```

`processor: spin` takes no parameters and may be written as a bare
name. `percent` requires a `language` and accepts an optional
`comment` marker (default `#`). An unknown processor name — or a
`percent` with no `language` — is a hard error at project load, never
a silently skipped file.

## Files that never render

Some files are excluded from the render list even when a pattern
matches them:

- files and directories whose name starts with `_` (partials,
  metadata) or `.` (hidden);
- anything under `node_modules/` or the output directory;
- `README` files (any extension, any capitalization);
- agent-instruction Markdown: `CLAUDE.md`, `CLAUDE.local.md`,
  `AGENTS.md`, `AGENTS.local.md`, and `*.llms.md` companions.

A render entry that names one of these — or that matches nothing at
all — produces a warning
([`Q-5-13`](/errors/project/Q-5-13.qmd)) so a silent gap in your site
doesn't go unnoticed.

Files inside a [nested project](#nested-projects) are also left out
unless a pattern names that directory.

## Nested projects

A subdirectory with its own `_quarto.yml` (or `_quarto.yaml`) is a
**nested project**, even inside another project and even when that
file has no `project:` key. Its files belong to it: `q2 render sub`
renders them with the nested config, and the outer project's render
list stops at the directory.

```
my-site/
├── _quarto.yml        ← outer project
├── index.qmd          ← in the outer render list
└── sub/
    ├── _quarto.yml    ← nested project: owns everything under sub/
    ├── index.qmd
    └── page.qmd
```

Whether a pattern reaches into `sub/` depends on whether it **names**
the directory. Look at the part of the pattern before its first
wildcard:

| Pattern | Reaches into `sub/`? |
|---------|----------------------|
| `**/*.qmd` (the default) | no |
| `**/*.md` | no |
| `*/page.qmd` | no, because `*` doesn't name `sub` |
| `sub/page.qmd` | yes |
| `sub/*.qmd` | yes |
| `sub/**/*.qmd` | yes |
| `sub` (bare directory) | yes |

When a pattern doesn't reach in, the nested project's files are left
out and Quarto warns once per render, listing every nested project it
skipped ([`Q-5-31`](/errors/project/Q-5-31.qmd)). A `!` pattern that
excludes the directory (e.g. `"!sub/**"`) silences the warning. You
have told Quarto the directory isn't part of this project.

When a pattern does reach in, the matched files render **as part of
the outer project, with the outer config**. The nested `_quarto.yml`
is not applied. Quarto warns about that too
([`Q-5-32`](/errors/project/Q-5-32.qmd)), because the same page
renders differently under `q2 render sub`.

A nested project inside a nested project is its own boundary. Naming
`sub` doesn't reach into `sub/deeper/` if that directory has its own
`_quarto.yml`.

Only `_quarto.yml` and `_quarto.yaml` mark a nested project. A
profile file such as `_quarto-prod.yml` on its own doesn't. To apply
settings to one directory of a project without splitting it off, use
`_metadata.yml`, which merges into every document in its directory
and leaves the directory in the outer project.

::: {.callout-note}
## Quarto 1 behaves differently

Quarto 1 ignores a nested `_quarto.yml` when rendering the outer
project, without any warning. It renders `sub/page.qmd` into the outer
site with the outer config, while `quarto render sub` renders it with
the nested config. If you migrate a site and pages under a
subdirectory go missing, check for a stray `_quarto.yml` there. Rename
it to `_metadata.yml` if it only held settings, or remove it if it's
left over.
:::

## Order

Positive patterns contribute files in the order you list them
(alphabetically within a single pattern). This is also the order pages
render in.
